introduction: On this Sunday, Amos warns those who lie on ivory beds and feast while caring nothing for the ruin of their people. In the Gospel, Jesus tells of the rich man who ignored the poor man Lazarus at his gate, and of the great chasm between them after death. Paul urges Timothy to fight the good fight of faith. Let us open our eyes to the Lazarus at our own gate.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord gives food to the hungry and raises up those who are bowed down. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may never forget the poor at her gate. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who live in luxury: that their hearts may be opened to the needs of others. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the homeless, the sick and the hungry, especially those whom no one sees: that they may be helped and comforted. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who have died, especially the poor and forgotten: that the angels may carry them to God. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may listen to God's word now and change our lives while there is time. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, you know every Lazarus by name. Open our eyes to the poor around us, and give us generous hearts, so that we may share the joy of your Kingdom. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: The poor man at the gate
reflection.body:
Amos speaks to the comfortable rich of Israel: "Woe to those who are at ease in Zion." They "lie on beds of ivory," eat the finest meat, drink wine by the bowlful, "but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph." Their sin is not only luxury but indifference to the suffering around them.

Jesus tells a parable that makes the same point unforgettable. A rich man, "clothed in purple and fine linen," feasts every day. At his gate lies a poor man, covered with sores, longing for the crumbs from his table. The poor man has a name: Lazarus, which means "God helps." The rich man has no name. We are not told that the rich man did anything cruel to Lazarus. He simply did not see him.

Both die. Lazarus is carried by angels to Abraham's side; the rich man finds himself in torment. Now he asks for help: "send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue!" Abraham reminds him that there is now "a great gulf fixed" between them. The gulf was there during his life too: the gate he never crossed.

The rich man begs Abraham to warn his five brothers. Abraham answers, "They have Moses and the prophets. Let them listen to them." When the rich man insists that a messenger from the dead would convince them, Abraham says, "If they don't listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded if one rises from the dead." We have God's word; we have the risen Christ. The question is whether we listen.

Paul tells Timothy: "Fight the good fight of faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called."

This week, ask who is lying at your gate: someone poor, lonely, sick, forgotten. See them, and cross the gate to help.
